taxonomy.name: Conflicting Information
taxonomy.definition: Includes two or more sources of information that conflict with each other. As a result, the user is unsure what the consequences of their actions will be and will be more likely to accept default settings that may not be in their best interest. Conflicting Information does not apply when one source explicitly uses conditional terms (“may,” “can,” “for example”). These terms allow the company to ask for additional information later without contradicting the initial statement.
taxonomy.exclusions: Do NOT label a case as Conflicting Information if one statement explicitly qualifies or limits another using reconciling language such as “except as described,” “subject to,” “as outlined above,” or clear section-specific scope indicators that logically reconcile the two statements.
examples: When attempting to submit a CCPA Right to Access request, the user is directed to a submission path described as supporting multiple CCPA rights, including the Right to Access. However, upon reaching the destination page, the webform explicitly supports only a limited subset of right requests, such as opt-out requests, and does not provide any option to submit an access request. This creates a direct contradiction between the instructional description and the available interface options, leaving the user uncertain about how to exercise the access right.

When a user clicks a link to exercise CCPA Right to Access, they are directed to a page titled/ or labeled as “Opt-Out” or “Do Not Sell”. Although the form may technically include options for accepting other rights, the prominent, contradictory title suggests the page is only for opting out. This creates a direct conflict between the user's intent and the page's framing, making the user unsure if they are in the correct place. If only the URL include opt-out but the page title is neutral, do NOT count it as this pattern.

When attempting to exercise the CCPA Right to Access, the user encounters conflicting instructions regarding how to submit the request. Specifically, multiple sources each present themselves as an CCPA designated submission method, yet one source indicates that requests can be submitted using a particular submission path or contact point, while another source provides a different or incompatible instruction for the same purpose, or states that certain listed submission paths are not valid. Because these sources give conflicting guidance, the user cannot determine which methods or submission paths are accepted.

When attempting to exercise the CCPA Right to Access, the user reviews the company’s privacy disclosures to understand what personal information is collected, shared, or sold about them. However, different sections of the disclosure provide contradictory statements, with one part indicating that the company collects a particular category of data and another stating that it does not, without any explicit scoping or qualifying language that reconciles the two (e.g., ‘except for’, or ‘subject to’). Because these disclosures conflict, the user cannot determine what personal information the company actually holds.

taxonomy.name: Information Without Context
taxonomy.definition: Alter the relevant information or user controls to limit discoverability. As a result, the user is unlikely to find the information or action possibility they are interested in.
examples: The privacy policy directs users to a single webform to exercise California privacy rights, including the Right to Access. However, the linked page does not actually allow users to submit an access request; instead, it supports only other rights (e.g., opt-out rights), is scoped to a different audience (e.g., B2B-only), or is otherwise unsuitable. Because the destination page does not match the scope implied by the instruction, users cannot use the webform to exercise their access rights, and must search for alternative methods, reducing the discoverability of the access pathway.

The privacy policy directs users to a single webform as the mechanism for exercising multiple California privacy rights, including the Right to Access. However, the linked page is titled or labeled as an opt-out request page (e.g., the page title “opt-out”), even though the page content technically supports access-related controls. Because the framing of the page does not match the expectations set by the policy, users may not recognize the page as relevant for exercising access rights, reducing discoverability. If only the URL include opt-out but the page title is neutral, do NOT count it as this pattern.

The privacy policy directs users to a webform to exercise California privacy rights, including Right to Access/Know. However, the form uses vague or non-standard request-type labels (e.g., “Right to Data Portability” or “Request Info”), while other rights may be labeled using clear legal terminology (e.g., “Right to Opt-out,” “Right to Erasure”). Because the request-type labels lack sufficient context to map to the user’s intended right, the availability of the access/know action becomes hard to discover.

The privacy policy directs users to locate information about CCPA under one section label (e.g., “CCPA privacy notice”), but the relevant information is actually presented under a differently titled section (e.g., “CCPA Addendum”), without any link or explanation indicating that the two refer to the same content. Because the referenced label does not match the actual section title, users are unlikely to locate the correct information, reducing discoverability.

A privacy policy includes a section framed as the comprehensive guide for CCPA rights and how to exercise them (e.g., “California Privacy Rights”, “Your Rights and Choices”, “Privacy Rights and Controls” or similar). However, this section does not include or link to the mechanism for submitting a Right to Access request. The actual submission method (e.g., an online webform, email, or phone number for access requests) appears only in a differently framed section such as “Contact Us”, “General Inquiries”, or even an opt-out/marketing choices page, without any reference or link from the comprehensive rights section. As a result, users who rely on the “comprehensive” section are unlikely to discover the correct action path, because the actionable information is presented in a location whose framing does not signal relevance to exercising access rights.

A company presents a section that is framed as a comprehensive for understanding how to exercise the CCPA Right to Access (e.g., “How to Exercise your Rights”, “California Privacy Rights”). This section provides incomplete or selectively scoped guidance, such as listing only certain submission methods (e.g., mail or email) or only certain steps, but omitting other valid methods or requirements. The omitted information (e.g., an online webform) appears only in a separate section with a different or unexpected focus (e.g., “Do Not Sell My Personal Information”) or on another page, without cross-reference. Because the placement of the omitted information is not intuitive for users to look for, and does not align with the expectations set by the comprehensive section, users are likely to rely on the partial guidance and overlook other available access pathways.

taxonomy.name: Forced Registration
taxonomy.definition: Subverts the user’s expectation that they can complete an action without registering or creating an account, instead tricking them into thinking that registration is required, often resulting in the sharing of unneeded personal data.
examples: A user attempts to submit a CCPA Right to Access request without registering or creating an account. During the process, the interface requires account credentials or otherwise steers the user into an account-based flow. In some cases, the company presents a “guest request” option, but selecting it leads to a webform that still enforces or strongly encourages registration before the request can be submitted.
